co_pagosa_springs.blurb: Pagosa Springs sits in southwestern Colorado along US 160 between Wolf Creek Pass and Bayfield, at about 7,000 feet. The climbing is scattered across many small crags rather than one big cliff. Sport and trad lead, with bouldering and a winter ice and mixed scene on the side. Grades center on 5.9 to 5.11, with a handful of easier routes and a short tail into the 5.12s. The Piedra River is the largest sub-area, a box canyon that stays cold and dark, with summer rock on its west side and ice in winter. New Dark Ages Crag, Waterfall Canyon and V-Mountain are the other larger crags.

sd_sylvan_lake.blurb: Sylvan Lake lies in Custer State Park in the Black Hills, at about 6,100 feet, and is the doorway to the Needles. The rock is sharp, strong granite, with spires and towers that have steep faces, quartz crystals in the surface, and cracks between. Trad leads, with a good amount of sport and bouldering. Most roped climbs run 5.6 to 5.12, with moderates well represented and a small group of harder routes. The face climbing is bold, often with widely spaced bolts, so a rack is useful even on bolted lines, and most summits are left by rappel. The Outlets hold the most climbs, followed by Middle Earth and Sylvan Lake Bouldering.

az_beardsley_bouldering.blurb: Beardsley Bouldering is a pile of granite boulders on a desert peak in north Phoenix, at about 1,570 feet. The granite is coarse and weathered. Every problem here is a boulder problem, and the grade spread leans easy: lots of V0 and below, a healthy middle in V3 to V5, and only a few lines past V7. Problems are mostly short, up to about 15 feet, and grades are described as old-school, so they can feel harder than the number suggests. A pad is worthwhile. The Main Bouldering Area and the Frontier Bouldering Area hold most of the problems, with smaller groups such as the Egg and Sunshine Boulder.

az_oak_creek_canyon.blurb: Oak Creek Canyon runs from the Flagstaff end near Pumphouse Wash down toward Sedona, with the highway along the canyon floor and many side canyons. Trad dominates, with a good amount of sport. Grades run heavy: most routes are 5.10 to 5.12, with a few easier ones and a hard end into 5.13. The Waterfall is by far the largest crag, a columnar basalt amphitheater of cracks and gear-protected faces, whose walls face different directions so some get early light and others afternoon sun. Insomnia Canyon is on sandstone, and Pumphouse Wash sandstone is soft. Cave Springs and Fire Wall add smaller crags.

md_harper_s_ferry.blurb: Harper's Ferry is where the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers meet, and the cliffs and boulders around it span Maryland, West Virginia and Virginia. The rock is hard quartzite, with good crack systems and positive edges on the faces. Bouldering makes up the largest share, followed by trad, with some top-rope climbing and a few sport routes. Boulder problems lie mostly between V0 and V5, and roped routes are mainly moderate, with a thinner run into 5.11 and 5.12. Maryland Heights is the tallest cliff in central Maryland, about 200 feet, and the largest trad area. The Tiers and the Highlands hold most of the boulders, and Balcony Rock offers shorter trad and top-rope.

ca_mount_st_helena.blurb: Mount St. Helena is in Napa wine country, and its crags overlook Napa Valley. The rock is volcanic and varies in form from crag to crag. Sport climbing is the main draw, with some trad and a little bouldering. Most routes fall between 5.7 and 5.11, with a decent range of easier ones and a small top end in the 5.12s. Reaching the crags takes a hike, and the farther areas are quieter. The Far Side has moderate grades and fewer people, while the Bear and the Satellite Rocks give more options.
